candidates.title: A small number of samples can poison LLMs
candidates.summary: Chapter 01 : Technical details A small number of samples can poison LLMs of any size Read the paper 01 Technical details 02 Results 03 Conclusions Published Oct 9, 2025 Team Alignment Topics Cybersecurity Training Scaling laws Partnerships Safeguards See more... In a joint study with the UK AI Security Institute and the Alan Turing Institute, we found that as few as 250 malicious documents can produce a "backdoor" vulnerability in a large language model—regardless of model size or training data volume. Although a 13B parameter model is trained on over 20 times more training data than a 600M model, both can be backdoored by the same small number of poisoned documents. Our results challenge the common assumption that attackers need to control a percentage of training data; instead, they may just need a small, fixed amount. Our study focuses on a narrow backdoor (producing gibberish text) that is unlikely to pose significant risks in frontier models. Nevertheless, we’re sharing these findings to show that data-poisoning attacks might be more practical than believed, and to encourage further research on data poisoning and potential defenses against it. candidates.summary: Redesigning source control at Anthropic Published Oct 13, 2026 Team Engineering Topics Coding Agents Productivity Claude Code See more... Updated October 15 to include more detail on the projects that pioneered many of the techniques we use in Scion. Related articles Product Feb 23, 2026 The making of Claude Code View more At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI. In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce. Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026. In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. candidates.title: Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude
candidates.summary: Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude Published Oct 16, 2026 Team Science Topics Discovery Coding Agents Research programs Claude Opus See more... Quantum computers will need carefully designed circuits to run useful algorithms on limited hardware. We gave Claude plain-language specifications for eight such circuits, drawn from chemistry, optimization, physics simulation, and number theory, along with an automated evaluator that checks and scores each design. Working largely on its own, Claude found designs that improve on the best published circuits, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more. Such improvements substantially reduce the quantum resources that useful applications require, so practical quantum computers could arrive sooner than previously anticipated. This work was led by Andi Gu as part of Anthropic’s STEM Fellows Program, with mentorship from Alek Kemeny, a quantum physicist at Anthropic, in collaboration with Susanne Yelin (Harvard University) and Mikhail Lukin (Harvard University and QuEra Computing). candidates.title: Announcing the Anthropic Economic Index Survey
candidates.summary: Announcing the Anthropic Economic Index Survey Published Apr 22, 2026 Team Economics Topics Economic Index Labor market How people use AI Economic Futures Productivity See more... Related articles Jun 26, 2026 Economic Index View more The Economic Research team is launching the Anthropic Economic Index Survey, a monthly survey conducted through Anthropic Interviewer . Understanding AI's economic impact requires moving beyond the quantitative data we have today. Usage and diffusion metrics tell us how AI is being deployed, and traditional labor market indicators—like employment rates, wage trends, and layoffs—track what has already happened, often with meaningful delay. Both are essential, but neither captures how people experience the changes to the economy that AI brings, nor what they expect to happen as AI capabilities advance. While AI is poised to have large effects, there is substantial uncertainty about how AI will affect jobs, productivity, and unemployment (and on what timeline). To forecast a transition that is still unfolding, we need to hear from the people who are living through it, and we need to do so on a cadence that can identify changes as they emerge. In the Anthropic Economic Index Survey, we aim to capture a rich new corpus of qualitative data. This effort complements a companion report that takes an economic lens to the 81,000 open-ended survey responses collected through Anthropic Interviewer in December.
